body:
in Film, Literature |   	November 24th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
Rank the films inspired by Edgar Allan Poe, and sev­er­al adap­ta­tions of “The Fall of the House of Ush­er” will almost cer­tain­ly come near the top. At first glance, that sto­ry of a man pay­ing a vis­it to an old friend who lives with his twin sis­ter in their fam­i­ly’s grand house — each of the lat­ter three well advanced into a dif­fer­ent process of dete­ri­o­ra­tion — might seem too short, as well as too light on con­flict to trans­late into a con­ven­tion­al screen­play. Yet it’s also full of cin­e­mat­i­cal­ly irre­sistible images, from the some­how ruinous yet whol­ly intact tit­u­lar man­sion to the blood­i­ly wretched sis­ter throw­ing her­self upon the ter­ri­fied broth­er who entombed her alive while their ances­tral home col­laps­es around them.
Of the twen­ty or thir­ty ver­sions of “The Fall of the House of Ush­er” so far made for the screen, the most cel­e­brat­ed remains the one Jean Epstein direct­ed in 1928. Offi­cial­ly des­ig­nat­ing it as one of the “great movies,” Roger Ebert calls that pic­ture’s vision of the great hall “one of the most haunt­ing spaces in the movies. Its floor is a vast mar­ble expanse, inter­rupt­ed here and there by an item of fur­ni­ture that seems dwarfed by the sur­round­ing empti­ness. An odd stair­case ris­es from one dis­tant cor­ner. It is not impos­si­ble that this vision, in one of the best-known French sur­re­al­ist films, inspired the design­ers of the great hall of Xanadu in Cit­i­zen Kane.”


	

The avant-garde film­mak­ing duo James Sib­ley Wat­son Jr. and Melville Web­ber (in col­lab­o­ra­tion with e. e. cum­mings, who con­tributed to the script) could hard­ly man­age the same scale of pro­duc­tion design for their own short adap­ta­tion of Poe’s sto­ry, which hap­pened to come out the same year.
But the result­ing Expres­sion­ist take on the mate­r­i­al has also been high­ly acclaimed, and through this YouTube playlist of Poe films, you can expe­ri­ence not just both of them, but also oth­er adap­ta­tions of “The Fall of the House of Ush­er” by idio­syn­crat­ic Czech ani­ma­tor Jan Švankma­jer and B‑movie pow­er­house Roger Cor­man. Sen­si­tive to Poe’s sen­sa­tion­al­ist appeal and air of trans­gres­sive deca­dence, Cor­man end­ed up direct­ing an eight-film “Poe cycle,” near­ly all of which star Vin­cent Price.


	

It’s fair to say that no film actor is more close­ly asso­ci­at­ed with Poe than Price, a link Tim Bur­ton cel­e­brat­ed in ani­ma­tion at the begin­ning of his career. Price even played the writer him­self in An Evening with Edgar Allan Poe, a spe­cial from 1970 in which he recites  “The Sphinx,” “The Cask of Amon­til­la­do,” “The Pit and the Pen­du­lum,” and “The Tell-Tale Heart.” That last, the most screen-adapt­ed Poe sto­ry of them all, also appears on the playlist in var­i­ous forms: an ear­ly D. W. Grif­fith fea­ture, the direc­to­r­i­al debut of Jules Dassin, an ani­mat­ed short nar­rat­ed by James Mason, a British psy­cho­log­i­cal thriller, and a trans­po­si­tion into mod­ern-day New Orleans. And if you haven’t had enough Poe after watch­ing through all 25 of these films, con­sid­er watch­ing the recent, well-received Fall of the House of Ush­er minis­eries on Net­flix — an enter­tain­ment plat­form that sat­is­fies much the same appetites Poe’s sto­ries have been feed­ing for near­ly two cen­turies.

title: Behold the Most Detailed Painting in History: The Ghent Altarpiece
description:
in Art, History |   	November 23rd, 2026  1 Comment

body:
in Art, History |   	November 23rd, 2026  1 Comment
	
			

	

These days, if you want to see a par­tic­u­lar paint­ing, you can almost cer­tain­ly pull it up online in sec­onds. In more and more cas­es, the res­o­lu­tion of the image will be so high that you can zoom in and in and in: such a lev­el of detail is unavail­able in a muse­um, of course, but also dif­fi­cult to access even if you owned the phys­i­cal art­work in ques­tion. Here on Open Cul­ture, we’ve pre­vi­ous­ly fea­tured such lux­u­ri­ant­ly dig­i­tized paint­ings as The Night Watch, Girl with a Pearl Ear­ring, and The Gar­den of Earth­ly Delights. But there’s at least one cel­e­brat­ed work of Dutch mas­ters whose view­ing expe­ri­ence can nev­er tru­ly be repli­cat­ed on the inter­net: the Ghent Altar­piece, also called the Ado­ra­tion of the Mys­tic Lamb, by Hubert and Jan van Eyck.
After watch­ing the video from The Gaze above, you’ll sure­ly want to take as close as pos­si­ble a look at the online Ghent Altar­piece, seek­ing out such high­light­ed details as the indi­vid­ual hairs on Adam’s beard, the real­is­ti­cal­ly awk­ward expres­sions on the faces of the angel cho­rus, and the iden­ti­fi­able cru­ci­fix­ion scene pinned to a pil­grim’s hat.
But that may only stoke your desire to make a pil­grim­age of your own, to Bel­gium, where you can see the real thing care­ful­ly placed in St. Bavo’s Cathe­dral. In the ear­ly fif­teenth cen­tu­ry, when that insti­tu­tion was called St. John the Bap­tist’s Church, its war­den was the wealthy mer­chant Jodocus Vijd. Hav­ing endowed a new chapel, Vijd also com­mis­sioned the van Eyck broth­ers to cre­ate an altar­piece spec­tac­u­lar enough to secure him a spot in the after­life. The result was one of the ear­li­est mas­ter­pieces of oil paint­ing.
Even apart from that des­ig­na­tion (to say noth­ing of its being the most stolen work of art in his­to­ry), it has enjoyed an impres­sive after­life of its own. Of the many who have trav­eled to behold it in situ at St. Bavo’s, some have no doubt sought the ecsta­sy of faith that can only be felt in a true holy place. But oth­ers have been thrilled, whether they were aware of it before­hand, by all the atten­tion the artists put into inte­grat­ing the work with its sur­round­ings. The light with­in its images, for exam­ple, is paint­ed in such a way as to match the light stream­ing into the cathe­dral itself. Those who look close­ly at the gem worn by the fore­most singing angel will see a reflec­tion of the very room meant for the altar. By the time their eyes meet the know­ing gaze of the sac­ri­fi­cial lamb, they’re all but guar­an­teed to have a reli­gious expe­ri­ence — though whether its nature is Chris­t­ian, artis­tic, or oth­er­wise will depend, as it does with all endur­ing art, on the indi­vid­ual view­er.

title: Marie Curie Became the First Woman to Win a Nobel Prize, the First Person to Win Twice, and the Only Person in History to Win in Two Different Sciences
description: For most of sci­en­tif­ic his­to­ry, women who made con­tri­bu­tions to var­i­ous fields have been side­lined or ignored in favor of male col­lea
body:
For most of sci­en­tif­ic his­to­ry, women who made con­tri­bu­tions to var­i­ous fields have been side­lined or ignored in favor of male col­leagues, who reaped fame, pro­fes­sion­al recog­ni­tion, and cash rewards that come with pres­ti­gious prizes like the Nobel. Cor­nell his­to­ri­an of sci­ence Mar­garet Rossiter coined the term “The Matil­da Effect” to describe sex­ist bias in the sci­ences. Rossiter’s work and pop­u­lar reap­praisals like book-turned-film Hid­den Fig­ures have inspired oth­er women in acad­e­mia to search for for­got­ten female sci­en­tists, and to find them, lit­er­al­ly, in foot­notes.
When sys­tem­at­ic dis­crim­i­na­tion lim­its oppor­tu­ni­ties for any group, those who do receive recog­ni­tion, the excep­tions to the rule, must often be tru­ly excep­tion­al to suc­ceed. There has been lit­tle doubt, both in her life­time and in the many decades after­ward, that Marie Curie was such a per­son. Although forced to study sci­ence in secret at a clan­des­tine “Float­ing Uni­ver­si­ty” in her native Poland—since the uni­ver­si­ties refused to admit women—Curie (born Marie Salomea Sklodows­ka in 1867) would achieve such renown in her field that she was award­ed not one, but two Nobel Prizes.
Curie and her hus­band Pierre shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with Antoine Hen­ri Bec­quer­el, dis­cov­er­er of radioac­tiv­i­ty, in 1903. The sec­ond prize, in Chem­istry, was hers alone in 1911, “in recog­ni­tion of her ser­vices to the advance­ment of chem­istry by the dis­cov­ery of the ele­ments radi­um and polo­ni­um, by the iso­la­tion of radi­um and the study of the nature and com­pounds of this remark­able ele­ment.” Curie was not only the first woman to win a Nobel, but she was also the first per­son to win twice, and the only per­son to win in two dif­fer­ent sci­ences.
These are but a hand­ful of achieve­ments in a string of firsts for Curie: denied posi­tions in Poland, she earned a Ph.D. in France, award­ed the degree in 1903 by the Sor­bonne, the same year she won her first Nobel. “Her exam­in­ers,” notes the site Famous Sci­en­tists, “were of the view that she had made the great­est con­tri­bu­tion to sci­ence ever found in a Ph.D. the­sis.” Three years lat­er, after Pierre was killed in an acci­dent, Marie was offered his pro­fes­sor­ship and became the first female pro­fes­sor at the Uni­ver­si­ty of Paris.
Curie suc­ceed­ed not in the absence of, but in spite of the sex­ist obsta­cles placed in her path at near­ly every stage in her career. After she received her doc­tor­ate, the Curies were invit­ed to the Roy­al Insti­tu­tion in Lon­don. Only Pierre was per­mit­ted to speak. That same year, the Nobel Com­mit­tee decid­ed to hon­or only her hus­band and Bec­quer­el. The Acad­e­my relent­ed when Pierre protest­ed. Curie fell vic­tim to a wave of xeno­pho­bia and anti-Semi­tism (though she was not Jew­ish) that swept through France in the 1900s, most famous­ly in the so-called “Drey­fus Affair.”
In 1911, the year of her sec­ond Nobel, Curie was passed over for mem­ber­ship in the French Acad­e­my of Sci­ences. It would take anoth­er 51 years before the first woman, Mar­guerite Perey, a for­mer doc­tor­al stu­dent of Curie, would be elect­ed to that body. That same year, Curie was per­se­cut­ed relent­less­ly by the French press, the pub­lic, and her sci­en­tif­ic rivals after it was revealed that she had had a brief affair with physi­cist Paul Langevin, one of Pierre Curie’s for­mer stu­dents.
But no mat­ter how many men in posi­tions of pow­er want­ed to deter Curie, there always seemed to be more influ­en­tial sci­en­tists and politi­cians who rec­og­nized the supreme val­ue of her work and the need to help her con­tin­ue it. After her sec­ond Nobel Prize, her native coun­try final­ly rec­og­nized her with the offer to direct her own lab­o­ra­to­ry in War­saw. Curie turned it down to focus on direct­ing the Curie Lab­o­ra­to­ry in the Radi­um Insti­tute of the Uni­ver­si­ty of Paris, which she found­ed in 1914, a major achieve­ment and, again, only a small part of her lega­cy.
Curie is known, of course, fore­most for her excep­tion­al sci­en­tif­ic work, but also for open­ing doors for women in sci­ence all over the world, though much of that door-open­ing may only have hap­pened decades after her death in 1934, and much of it hasn’t hap­pened at all yet. Inci­den­tal­ly, in the fol­low­ing year, the Curies’ daugh­ter Irène Joliot-Curie and her hus­band Frédéric Joliot-Curie were joint­ly award­ed the Nobel Prize in Chem­istry. Since then, only sev­en oth­er women have claimed that hon­or, and only five women, includ­ing Marie Curie, have won the Prize in physics, out of 230 win­ners total.
There may be noth­ing yet like gen­der par­i­ty in the sci­ences, but those who know where to look can find the names of dozens of women sci­en­tists run­ning women-owned com­pa­nies, women-found­ed research insti­tutes and aca­d­e­m­ic depart­ments, and, like the famous Curies, mak­ing major con­tri­bu­tions to chem­istry. Per­haps not long from now, many of those excep­tion­al sci­en­tists will be as well-known and wide­ly cel­e­brat­ed as Marie Curie.
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2019.

title: How Isaac Newton Lost $3 Million Dollars in the “South Sea Bubble” of 1720: Even Geniuses Can’t Prevail Against the Machinations of the Markets
description: The Aris­totelian notion of “man” as a “ratio­nal ani­mal” has seen its share of detrac­tors, from the Cyn­ics to Bertrand Rus­sell to near­ly th
body:
The Aris­totelian notion of “man” as a “ratio­nal ani­mal” has seen its share of detrac­tors, from the Cyn­ics to Bertrand Rus­sell to near­ly the whole of Post­struc­tural­ist thought. Leave it up to Oscar Wilde to com­press the debate between intel­lect and pas­sion into a pithy apho­rism: “Man is a ratio­nal ani­mal who always los­es his tem­per when he is called upon to act in accor­dance with the dic­tates of rea­son.”
We no longer need clever ver­bal barbs to refute too-opti­mistic assess­ments of human behav­ior. Eco­nom­ics is catch­ing up: we have the lan­guage of neu­ro­science and psy­chol­o­gy, which con­sis­tent­ly tells us that humans decid­ed­ly do not behave ratio­nal­ly very often, but are dri­ven by bias and biol­o­gy in inex­plic­a­ble ways. And for over a hun­dred years now, we’ve known that the clock­work New­ton­ian view of the phys­i­cal uni­verse turns out to be a much messier and inde­ter­mi­nate affair, as does the uni­verse of the human mind.
Why, then, has so much eco­nom­ic the­o­ry oper­at­ed with a kind of dogged Aris­totelian­ism, insist­ing that the units of cap­i­tal­ist soci­ety, the work­ers, man­agers, investors, con­sumers, own­ers, renters, spec­u­la­tors, etc. behave in pre­dictable ways? We have case after case show­ing that intel­li­gence and crit­i­cal rea­son­ing often have lit­tle to do with suc­cess or fail­ure in the mar­ket. In such cas­es, how­ev­er, one often hears the “mad­ness of crowds” or oth­er clichés invoked as an expla­na­tion.
To illus­trate, mar­ket reporters and busi­ness writ­ers have seized upon the sto­ry of Isaac Newton’s spec­tac­u­lar rise and fall in the so-called “South Sea Bub­ble” of 1720. We find the sto­ry in Ben­jamin Graham’s 1949 clas­sic The Intel­li­gent Investor, a wide­ly-read book that attrib­ut­es the irra­tional­i­ty of mar­ket sys­tems to an anthro­po­mor­phic enti­ty named “Mr. Mar­ket.”
Gra­ham writes,
Back in the spring of 1720, Sir Isaac New­ton owned shares in the South Sea Com­pa­ny, the hottest stock in Eng­land. Sens­ing that the mar­ket was get­ting out of hand, the great physi­cist mut­tered that he ‘could cal­cu­late the motions of the heav­en­ly bod­ies, but not the mad­ness of the peo­ple.’ New­ton dumped his South Sea shares, pock­et­ing a 100% prof­it total­ing £7,000. But just months lat­er, swept up in the wild enthu­si­asm of the mar­ket, New­ton jumped back in at a much high­er price — and lost £20,000 (or more than $3 mil­lion in [2002–2003’s] mon­ey. For the rest of his life, he for­bade any­one to speak the words ‘South Sea’ in his pres­ence.
The quo­ta­tion in bold may or may not have been uttered by New­ton, but the events Gra­ham describes did indeed hap­pen. As the Wall Street Jour­nal’s Jason Zweig relates, Uni­ver­si­ty of Min­neso­ta pro­fes­sor Andrew Odlyzko found that “New­ton had shift­ed from a pru­dent investor with his mon­ey spread across sev­er­al secu­ri­ties to a spec­u­la­tor who had plunged essen­tial­ly all of his cap­i­tal into a sin­gle stock. The great sci­en­tist was chas­ing hot per­for­mance as des­per­ate­ly as a day trad­er in 1999 or many bit­coin buy­ers in 2017.” (Odlyzko esti­mates New­ton’s loss­es at clos­er to $4 mil­lion.) Per­haps it was not a metaphor­i­cal “Mr. Mar­ket” who cost New­ton up to 77% “on his worst pur­chas­es,” nor was it wide­spread “wild enthusiasm”—the mass move­ment of pas­sion that Enlight­en­ment philoso­phers so feared.
Per­haps it was New­ton him­self who, Ele­na Holod­ny writes at Busi­ness Insid­er, “let his emo­tions get the best of him, and got swayed by the irra­tional­i­ty of the crowd.” Maybe it’s more accu­rate to say New­ton suc­cumbed to greed when the bub­ble expand­ed. “Through­out his­to­ry,” Bar­bara Kollmey­er writes at Mar­ket Watch in her inter­view with author Richard Dale, “people—especially those at the top rung of society—have been greedy and gullible par­tic­i­pants in finan­cial bub­bles. And Sir Isaac New­ton was only human, after all.” (How many at the top rung of soci­ety fell prey to Bernie Madoff’s schemes? And a cen­tu­ry before the South Sea Bub­ble, hun­dreds of wealthy investors lost their shirts in the Dutch Tulip Bulb craze.)
Some busi­ness writ­ers, like invest­ment edi­tor Richard Evans at The Tele­graph, rec­om­mend a cal­cu­la­ble for­mu­la to avoid los­ing a for­tune in bub­bles, advice that takes ratio­nal agency for grant­ed. Per­haps it should not. In addi­tion to cit­ing the con­ta­gion of crowds, near­ly every dis­cus­sion of Newton’s fol­ly allows that a fail­ure of emo­tion­al dis­ci­pline played a sig­nif­i­cant role. Ben­jamin Gra­ham invokes anoth­er Aris­totelian notion—the idea that “char­ac­ter” counts as much or more than intel­li­gence when it comes to invest­ing. “The investor’s chief prob­lem,” he writes, “and even his worst enemy—is like­ly to be him­self.”
Far few­er com­menters note that the South Sea ven­ture was itself a fail­ure of char­ac­ter from its incep­tion. The com­pa­ny had secured an exclu­sive monop­oly on trade with South Amer­i­ca; much of that trade involved sell­ing slaves. It is also the case that the com­pa­ny arti­fi­cial­ly inflat­ed its stock prices, and col­lud­ed with sev­er­al MPs in insid­er trad­ing schemes. The so-called “Bub­ble Act” of Par­lia­ment in 1720, pre­sum­ably passed to pre­vent crash­es like the one that dev­as­tat­ed New­ton, turned out to be a cor­po­rate give­away. The terms of the act had been dic­tat­ed by the South Sea Com­pa­ny in order to pre­vent oth­er com­pa­nies from poach­ing their investors. Although these cir­cum­stances are well-known to eco­nom­ic his­to­ri­ans, they rarely make their way into com­men­tary on Newton’s great loss.
Econ­o­mists instead tend to blame abstrac­tions for eco­nom­ic events like the South Sea Bub­ble, or they blame the over­reach­ing prof­it-seek­ing of investors, and maybe for good rea­son. The oth­er expla­na­tions haunt the mar­gins: the inher­ent­ly exploita­tive nature of most forms of cor­po­rate cap­i­tal­ism, and the cor­rup­tion and col­lu­sion between the state and pri­vate enter­prise that inhibits fair com­pe­ti­tion and makes it impos­si­ble for investors to eval­u­ate the sit­u­a­tion trans­par­ent­ly. For all of his sci­en­tif­ic and math­e­mat­i­cal genius, Isaac New­ton was no exception—he was just as sub­ject to irra­tional greed as the next investor, and to the preda­to­ry machi­na­tions of “mar­ket forces.”
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2018.

Catherine Lepage will have you leaping out of your desk chair with her self-directed “Dancing on Osees.” The irresistible animation features a quirky troupe of characters who can’t help but get down to “Together Tomorrow.” As the energetic track bolts forward, so do the hand-drawn dancers, who Lepage captures through stop-motion collages on paper.
The Montréal-based artist graciously shares glimpses behind the scenes on Instagram.

title: Six Artworks Under $1,000 We'd Love to Give (and Receive!) This Holiday
description: There’s an unparalleled joy in watching a loved one unwrap something they both never anticipated and immediately know they’ve needed all along. Th
body:
There’s an unparalleled joy in watching a loved one unwrap something they both never anticipated and immediately know they’ve needed all along. These types of gifts are often the most unexpected, surprisingly personal, and typically, one of a kind.
Our partners at Joy Machine have generously curated a selection of artworks that fit this category. Priced under $1,000, the collection includes pieces by an international group of artists that longtime Colossal readers will surely recognize. From playful drawings in walnut ink to uncanny kitsch sculptures, these works are perfecting for gifting this holiday season, even (especially?) if that gift is to yourself.
Seattle-based artist Debra Broz applies her training in ceramic conservation to a practice that involves scouring flea markets and thrift shops for ceramic figurines, breaking their forms, and reassembling the figures as surreal hybrids. 
Collect “Boxer Horse” ($750)
Collin van der Sluijs, “White Line Sphinx Moth drawing” (2026), mixed media on paper, framed, 8.3 x 11.7 inches
Dutch artist Collin van der Sluijs is a master of several styles, with a background in graffiti and street art and a parallel interest in the delicate, impeccably detailed features of the natural world.
Collect “White Line Sphinx Moth drawing” ($550)
Stevie Shao, “Star Bull” (2025), acrylic gouache and latex paint on paper, 21 x 21 centimeters
With a deep love for the flora and fauna near her home in the Pacific Northwest, Stevie Shao creates folk art-inspired works through bold color palettes and arresting patterns.
Collect “Star Bull” ($400)
Misato Sano, “レッツ ワークアウト！ / Let’s work out!” (2025), drawing paper, acrylic gouache, walnut ink, 11 x 14 inches (framed)
Japanese artist Misato Sano is best known for her cheeky wooden carvings of poodles and pugs, which she translates to two-dimensions in this playful rendition that might just make us want to get up and get moving.
Collect “Let’s work out” ($150)
Danym Kwon, “A Quiet Afternoon” (2026), acrylic gouache on birch plywood, 11 x 5 x 1.125 inches
Through large-scale paintings and small woodcuts, Danym Kwon meditates on the mundane activities like folding laundry or strolling around the park that allow memories to emerge and be understood anew.
Collect “A Quiet Afternoon” ($350)
Rachel Hayden, “Halloween in May”(2026), acrylic on panel, 8 x 10 inches
Layering acrylic paint with crisp edges that evoke paper collage, Rachel Hayden blends the patterns of a summertime picnic with the eerie colors and atmosphere of fall, perfect for the perpetually witchy pal.
Collect “Halloween in May” ($900)

title: Su Blackwell Enchants with Folkloric Stories That Spring from Vintage Books
description: From vintage tomes and encyclopedic volumes, British artist Su Blackwell carves, slices, and reconfigures text-laden pages into enchanting sculptu
body:
From vintage tomes and encyclopedic volumes, British artist Su Blackwell carves, slices, and reconfigures text-laden pages into enchanting sculptures. Her latest body of work, opening this week in a solo show titled Pathway of Crumbs, draws on fairytales and folklore, a fitting topic for such dreamlike scenes.
Nodding to the enduring children’s story of Hansel and Gretel, the exhibition roots in nature and the stories we draw from the world around us. “In Flight,” for example, stretches nearly 3.5 feet as a swarm of butterflies emerges from the flared pages of a book. “Break off my Branches” is similarly dynamic, with a flock of multi-colored birds perched on the spindly stems that burst from a splayed edition. 
“Break off my Branches” (2025), paper cut sculpture and wooden frame without glass, 115 x 16 x 85 centimeters
Blackwell selected this particular set of books because they’ve been in her collection for several years, allowing the artist to digest their contents and ruminate on how they might emerge over time. Some she’s left in the same condition since purchasing them from a secondhand shop, and others she’s minimally cut and spliced for earlier projects. All, though, have remained a compelling artifact of human knowledge and a collective desire to create, one she transforms anew into striking compositions at the intersection of nature and culture.
Pathway of Crumbs is on view from November 25 to January 25 at Long & Ryle in London. Find more from Blackwell on her website.
